config.title: Build optimistic concurrency control endpoint

intro.title: Build optimistic concurrency control endpoint
intro.body: In this lesson, you will build a Node.js API endpoint that implements optimistic concurrency control. This technique prevents data conflicts when multiple users try to update the same resource simultaneously, without locking the database. You will learn to use version numbers (like timestamps or counters) to detect and handle update collisions. The main technologies involved are Express.js for routing, a simple in-memory data store, and conditional logic in JavaScript. By the end, you'll have a functional endpoint that safely manages concurrent updates in a web application.
intro.usecase: Optimistic concurrency control is essential in collaborative editing tools like Google Docs or Figma, where multiple users edit the same document simultaneously. It prevents data loss when two users submit conflicting changes to shared resources like project management tickets in Jira or Trello cards. This pattern also protects inventory systems in e-commerce platforms during high-traffic sales events, ensuring customers don't oversell limited stock items. Developers implement these endpoints to maintain data integrity in any multi-user application where race conditions could corrupt critical business data.

objectives: Implement a version tracking mechanism for data entities
Construct an endpoint that validates client-supplied version numbers
Apply conditional logic to handle version conflicts in update operations
Configure HTTP response codes for successful updates and version conflicts
Manipulate data persistence only when version checks pass
Integrate version validation middleware into the request flow
Initialize version tracking for new data entities

steps.instruction: Create an HTTP server using http.createServer() and define a request handling function that logs the request method and URL.

steps.hint: Use the url.parse() method on the request.url property to get a URL object, then access its pathname. The HTTP method is available as request.method.
steps.expectedOutcome: The server handler will be able to identify which resource is being requested and what action (GET, PUT, etc.) should be performed.
successCriteria: The request handler contains code that parses req.url to get pathname and accesses req.method.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.

steps.title: Handle GET requests to retrieve items
steps.instruction: Inside the request handler, add an if statement to check if the request method is 'GET' and the pathname starts with '/items/'. If true, extract the item ID from the pathname and retrieve the item from dataStore.items.
steps.hint: Use req.method and parsedUrl.pathname to check the request. The item ID will be after '/items/' in the pathname. Access the item with dataStore.items[id].
steps.expectedOutcome: The server will now detect GET requests to item endpoints and extract the item ID for retrieval.
successCriteria: An if statement checks for GET method and '/items/' pathname, extracts the item ID, and attempts to retrieve it from dataStore.items.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure you're checking both the method and pathname, and extracting the ID correctly.
steps.feedbackWrong: The GET request handling isn't implemented correctly. Check the method, pathname, and ID extraction.

steps.expectedOutcome: The server will be able to receive and parse JSON request bodies for PUT operations.

steps.feedbackWrong: The request body collection logic is missing or incorrect. Remember to accumulate body chunks and parse JSON specifically for PUT requests.

steps.title: Implement optimistic concurrency check
steps.instruction: Inside the server request handler, add logic to compare the client-provided version from the request body with the server's current version before allowing an update.
steps.hint: Check if the version in the request body matches the version stored in dataStore.versions for that item ID.
steps.expectedOutcome: The server will now compare versions before processing updates, preventing conflicts when multiple clients try to update the same item.
successCriteria: Code includes a version comparison check that returns a 409 conflict response when versions don't match.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure you're comparing the client version from the request body with the server version from dataStore.versions.
steps.feedbackWrong: The optimistic concurrency check isn't implemented correctly. You need to compare versions and return a 409 response when they don't match.

steps.title: Handle successful updates with version increment
steps.instruction: Inside the request handler, after the optimistic concurrency check, add the update logic that runs when version numbers match. This should update the item in dataStore.items and increment its version in dataStore.versions.
steps.hint: When the client's version matches the stored version, update the item's data and increment the version number by 1 for future requests.
steps.expectedOutcome: The server will now properly handle successful updates by modifying the stored item and incrementing its version number when the client's version matches.
successCriteria: The update logic is implemented inside the request handler, updates dataStore.items, and increments dataStore.versions when version numbers match.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You've added some update logic, but make sure you're both updating the item in dataStore.items and incrementing the version in dataStore.versions when the client version matches the stored version.
steps.feedbackWrong: The update logic with version increment isn't properly implemented. Look at the analogous example - you need to check if versions match, then update the item data and increment the version number.

steps.title: Handle concurrency conflicts with error response
steps.instruction: In the server's request handler, add an else clause after the optimistic concurrency check to return a 409 Conflict response when the client's version doesn't match the server's version.
steps.hint: After checking if (clientVersion === serverVersion), add an else block that sets the response status code to 409 and sends a JSON error message.
steps.expectedOutcome: The server will properly respond with a 409 status code and error message when a client tries to update an item with an outdated version.
successCriteria: The else clause returns a 409 status with a JSON error object when version mismatch occurs.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure you're setting the status code to 409 and returning a JSON error message in the else block.
steps.feedbackWrong: The concurrency conflict handling isn't quite right. You need to add an else clause after the version check that returns a 409 status with a JSON error object.
